## The Southern Slope of Sierra Nevada

On the southern slope of Sierra Nevada, the plant landscape is rearranging itself with a slowness that only scientific instruments can capture. The *Sierra Nevada Global Change* project, driven by the CSIC, has documented a phenomenon that the shepherds of the Alpujarra have sensed for decades: the plants are moving up. Forty-five species have ascended an average of two hundred meters in altitude since 1980, a silent shift that alters the physiognomy of slopes, ravines, and peaks. The data come from the Experimental Station of Arid Zones, based in Almería, whose researchers have been measuring the distribution of flora in this mountain range for four decades.

The mechanism is as simple as it is relentless. As average temperatures rise, the conditions once found at fifteen hundred meters are now reproduced at seventeen hundred, and species that depend on a specific thermal range have no choice but to move upward. The problem is that the mountain is finite: those living at the summit have nowhere to go. The creeping juniper, that stunted conifer that colonizes the high peaks with admirable tenacity, is retreating because its climatic niche narrows year after year. The snow star, a white-flowered plant that grows in the snowbeds and high-mountain scree, suffers the same pressure: its habitat is shrinking like a sinking island.

In the middle Alpujarra, between one thousand and fifteen hundred meters, the change manifests itself in a different way. The quejigo, a semi-marcescent oak that prefers cool soils and shaded areas, is replacing the holm oak on many slopes where the latter has dominated for centuries. This is not a sudden invasion, but a gradual transition: young quejigos appear in the clearings of the holm oak forest, grow in the shade of the old holm oaks, and when these die, they take their place. Botanists interpret this replacement as a sign that the climate in the Alpujarra is becoming more humid in the middle zones, or at least less extreme in its summers, which favors species that were previously relegated to the shadiest ravines.

The upward shift of the flora is neither a uniform process nor free of contradictions. While some species gain ground, others lose it with no possibility of compensation. High-mountain plants, adapted to long winters and short summers, cannot compete with those arriving from lower elevations, which are more aggressive and better equipped to exploit nutrients. The result is a net loss of biodiversity at the summits, where the number of endemic species decreases in favor of a more generalist flora. CSIC researchers have warned that this impoverishment also affects pollinating insects, which depend on specific flowers at specific times of the year.

For the inhabitants of the Alpujarra, these changes have practical consequences that go beyond botanical interest. The shepherds who take their livestock up to the high-altitude pastures observe how the meadows are covered with scrub earlier than usual, while beekeepers notice variations in flowering that alter the calendar of their hives. Chestnut honey, one of the emblematic products of the region, depends on trees that are also modifying their altitudinal distribution. The chestnut trees, introduced by the Romans and consolidated by the Arabs, are now found in a higher band than half a century ago, which forces a rethinking of the location of traditional apiaries.

The scientific monitoring of these shifts is carried out through permanent plots distributed along the entire altitudinal gradient of Sierra Nevada. Each plot is precisely marked and periodically reviewed to record which species appear, which disappear, and how the density of each varies. This fieldwork, which requires hiking up to elevations above three thousand meters with measuring equipment, has made it possible to build an unprecedented historical series in southern Europe. The data collected since 1980 show that the rate of ascent has accelerated in the last two decades, coinciding with the warmest summers recorded on the peninsula.

The replacement of the holm oak by the quejigo in the middle Alpujarra also has a landscape reading. The quejigo loses its leaves in winter, unlike the holm oak, which keeps its green canopy all year round. This means that the slopes where the quejigo is advancing take on an ochre tone in the cold months, a chromatic change that the most observant already perceive from the viewpoints of the region. Forestry technicians consulted by the CSIC point out that this transformation is not necessarily negative from an ecological point of view, since the quejigo adds more organic matter to the soil and favors the presence of certain forest birds. However, it implies a profound alteration of the traditional ecosystems of dehesa and Mediterranean woodland.

The case of the creeping juniper is especially illustrative of the limits of adaptation. This species, which grows close to the ground to resist wind and frost, has tried to colonize higher areas as its habitat warmed. But above three thousand meters, the soil is too scarce, the ultraviolet radiation too intense, and the growing season too short. The juniper thus finds itself trapped between a lower belt that no longer offers it suitable conditions and an upper belt that it cannot conquer. Scientists call this situation the "summit effect" and consider it one of the main threats to high-mountain flora throughout the Mediterranean.

The snow star, whose scientific name is *Plantago nivalis*, exemplifies the fragility of species linked to snowbeds. These plants depend on the moisture that is slowly released when the snow melts, a resource that is decreasing in duration and intensity. The snowbeds of Sierra Nevada, which once lasted well into the summer, now disappear weeks earlier, and with them the life cycle of these plants is shortened. Botanists have found that the snow star blooms earlier each year, a phenological advance that can desynchronize it from its natural pollinators and compromise its reproduction.

The *Sierra Nevada Global Change* project is not limited to documenting the problem, but also proposes adaptive management measures. Among these is the creation of micro-reserves in the highest areas, where relict populations of threatened flora are protected, and the collection of seeds for their conservation in germplasm banks. These actions, coordinated with the Natural Space of Sierra Nevada, seek to buy time while the real scope of climate change in the mountains becomes clear. Researchers insist that the Alpujarra is a privileged observatory for understanding what will happen in other Mediterranean mountain ranges over the coming decades.

The upward displacement of the flora is, ultimately, a one-way migration that is rewriting the botanical map of the region. Where holm oaks once grew, quejigos now sprout; where the creeping juniper carpeted the summits, bare scree remains. The mountain, which for centuries seemed immutable, now reveals itself as a living organism that responds to every tenth of a degree of temperature increase. The CSIC data confirm this with the coldness of the figures: two hundred meters of ascent in four decades, forty-five species on the move, a landscape changing before the eyes of those who know how to look.
